name: Degree So with a Result Content Clause

entry.name: Degree So with a Result Content Clause

1.definition: Identifies a high degree through a resulting or evidentially linked situation.

examples.form: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn’t turn].

relatedConstructions.notes: So cold that the locks froze has degree marking on an adjective. Such a cold morning that the locks froze uses a nominal expression. Both specify degree or kind through a stated result.

projection.target: The result clause identifies the relevant scale threshold and ordinarily presents a realized situation. Compare too narrow to turn, which describes an obstacle without reporting an attempt.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: So much that something happens
curious.summary: So plus a describing word, followed by a clause about a resulting or linked situation, shows how high a degree is.
curious.body:
The street was so narrow that the van couldn't turn. The word so marks a high degree of narrowness, and the part after that tells what resulted. That result shows how narrow the street was.

The result clause sets the level that counts. It ordinarily presents something that really happened. Compare too narrow to turn, which describes an obstacle without reporting that anyone tried. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn't turn].
The soup was [so hot that she couldn't eat it].

curious.try: Finish this: The room was so cold that ... What result shows how cold it was?

teacher.summary: Helps explain so plus an adjective plus a that-clause that gives a result.
teacher.explain: The pattern is so plus a gradable expression plus a content clause, in which that is optional. It identifies a high degree through a resulting or evidentially linked situation. The result clause identifies the relevant scale threshold and ordinarily presents a realized situation. Compare too narrow to turn, which describes an obstacle without reporting an attempt. This dictionary also notes the overlap with such a cold morning that the locks froze, where the degree is specified through a nominal expression instead of an adjective. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: The that-clause is a declarative content clause; the that may be omitted.

examples.text: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn't turn].
The soup was [so hot that she couldn't eat it].

contrasts.text: The street was so narrow that the van couldn't turn.
contrasts.note: The result is presented as having happened.

contrasts.text: The street was too narrow to turn in.
contrasts.note: An obstacle is described, and no attempt is reported.

contrasts.text: It was such a cold morning that the locks froze.

watch_for: A learner might read the that-clause as a separate sentence, when it states the situation linked to the degree.
A learner might use too narrow to turn when a reported result is wanted.
teacher.activity: Give students adjectives (cold, noisy, heavy). They write a so ... that sentence with a realized result, then rewrite it with too ... to and say how the meaning shifts.

child.hook: How would you show that something was REALLY hot?
child.explain: You can say how much by saying what happened. The street was so narrow that the van couldn't turn. The result shows how narrow it was.

examples.text: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn't turn].
The soup was [so hot that she couldn't eat it].

child.play: Finish the sentence The box was so heavy that ... in three different ways.

checked.note: Fixed: the optional element is the word that, not the whole clause; curious summary no longer implies the clause must be introduced by that or that the degree causes the situation (the entry allows a resulting or evidentially linked situation); watch_for no longer treats a clause without a causal result as a learner error. Dismissed: none.
